title: Applying `#[\Attribute]` to an abstract class, enum, interface, or trait becomes a compile-time error
summary: As of PHP 8.5, marking an abstract class, an enum, an interface, or a trait with `#[\Attribute]` (making it usable as `#[ThatName]` elsewhere) is rejected during compilation. Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19, all four of these declarations compile today with zero diagnostics, and a class decorated with the resulting attribute reflects a normal, present `ReflectionAttribute` - the failure only surfaces when `ReflectionAttribute::newInstance()` (or anything else that tries to instantiate the attribute class) is actually called, at which point each of the four throws the exact same `Error` a bare `new` of that class-like would throw. PHP 8.5 moves that same failure to compile time; a new `#[\DelayedTargetValidation]` attribute can defer it back to runtime.
new_code_policy: Only mark a class with `#[\Attribute]` if that class is a plain, concrete, instantiable class - never an `abstract class`, an `enum`, an `interface`, or a `trait`. On a PHP 8.5+ floor this is enforced immediately, at compile time, for every file that declares such a combination, regardless of whether anything ever calls `ReflectionAttribute::newInstance()` on it. If a library genuinely needs an attribute-provider class to stay abstract/enum/interface/trait-shaped and wants the previous, lazy-at-`newInstance()`-time behavior back, PHP 8.5 adds `#[\DelayedTargetValidation]` for exactly that - but reach for it deliberately, not as a default: it is a PHP 8.5-only attribute (unavailable to write in a codebase with a floor below 8.5), and it only postpones the same eventual failure to runtime rather than removing it, so choosing it still means shipping a class that cannot actually be instantiated as the attribute it claims to be.
existing_code_policy:
Search for `#[\Attribute]` applied to a class-like declaration and check whether that declaration is `abstract`, `enum`, `interface`, or `trait`. Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19: all four combinations - `#[\Attribute] abstract class`, `#[\Attribute] enum`, `#[\Attribute] interface`, and `#[\Attribute] trait` - compile with zero diagnostics, and a class decorated with `#[ThatAttribute]` reports exactly one entry from `(new ReflectionClass(...))->getAttributes()`; nothing looks wrong until something actually tries to instantiate the attribute. Calling `newInstance()` on that one entry throws, for every one of the four kinds, the identical `Error` that a bare `new` of the same class-like already throws today: `Cannot instantiate abstract class {Name}`, `Cannot instantiate enum {Name}`, `Cannot instantiate interface {Name}`, and `Cannot instantiate trait {Name}` respectively - confirming `newInstance()` does not raise a distinct "invalid attribute target" message of its own; it just reaches the ordinary instantiation failure lazily.

On a PHP 8.5+ floor this exact combination stops compiling at all, so the fix is not optional there; on any floor, treat it as a bug to fix now rather than wait for the newer, stricter enforcement: either the attribute-provider class was mistakenly declared as abstract/enum/interface/trait and should become a plain concrete class (verify nothing else in the codebase depends on it being an interface to `implements`, a trait to `use`, or an enum for its case syntax before doing this - those are breaking changes of their own, not part of this rule), or the pattern was never meant to be instantiated as an attribute and the `#[\Attribute]` marking itself should be removed. Moving this failure from a lazy runtime `Error` to an eager compile-time one is, in general, an improvement - it turns a bug that could ship silently, as long as nothing ever called `newInstance()` on that class, into one caught immediately - but it is still a real deployment consequence for any code currently relying on the lazy behavior: a file that loads and runs correctly today, because it never exercises `newInstance()` on the affected class, will fail to compile at all on PHP 8.5, unconditionally, the moment that floor is reached.
guideline: Apply `#[\Attribute]` only to a plain, concrete class - never to an `abstract class`, `enum`, `interface`, or `trait`. Verified directly, all four invalid combinations compile silently on PHP 8.4.19 and only fail once `ReflectionAttribute::newInstance()` is actually called, throwing the same `Cannot instantiate {abstract class|enum|interface|trait} {Name}` error a bare `new` would; PHP 8.5 raises that same error at compile time instead, unconditionally, whether or not anything ever calls `newInstance()`. `#[\DelayedTargetValidation]` (PHP 8.5-only) can restore the old lazy timing deliberately, but does not remove the underlying failure.
details:
UPGRADING-8.5.0 lists this under Backward Incompatible Changes -> Core: "Applying #[\Attribute] to an abstract class, enum, interface, or trait triggers an error during compilation. Previously, the attribute could be added, but when ReflectionAttribute::newInstance() was called an error would be thrown. The error can be delayed from compilation to runtime using the new #[\DelayedTargetValidation] attribute."

Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19, with `set_error_handler()` installed (no diagnostic was raised anywhere in this sequence): all four of `#[\Attribute] abstract class AbstractAttr {}`, `#[\Attribute] enum EnumAttr { case A; }`, `#[\Attribute] interface InterfaceAttr {}`, and `#[\Attribute] trait TraitAttr {}` compile cleanly, as do target classes decorated with each of `#[AbstractAttr]`, `#[EnumAttr]`, `#[InterfaceAttr]`, and `#[TraitAttr]`. Reflecting any one of those target classes reports `getAttributes()` count `1` in every case - the attribute looks entirely present and healthy. Calling `newInstance()` on that one `ReflectionAttribute`, however, throws for every one of the four: `Error: Cannot instantiate abstract class AbstractAttr`, `Error: Cannot instantiate enum EnumAttr`, `Error: Cannot instantiate interface InterfaceAttr`, `Error: Cannot instantiate trait TraitAttr` - and a bare `new AbstractAttr()` / `new EnumAttr()` / `new InterfaceAttr()` / `new TraitAttr()`, tried directly outside of any attribute machinery, throws the byte-for-byte identical message in each case. `ReflectionAttribute::newInstance()` therefore does not perform any attribute-specific target validation of its own on this host; it simply attempts the same `new $attributeClass(...)` any other caller would, and inherits whatever that ordinary instantiation attempt throws. PHP 8.5 moves that exact check from "whenever something calls `newInstance()`" to "unconditionally, at compile time, the moment `#[\Attribute]` is seen on one of these four kinds of declaration" - a class that would have compiled and run for years without incident, simply because nothing in it ever called `newInstance()` on the mismarked class, stops compiling at all on 8.5.

Moving a failure from being reachable-but-lazy to being unconditional-and-immediate is usually a net improvement in reliability - the bug is now impossible to ship silently - but it is a real, one-directional deployment consequence: code that loads today keeps loading right up until the floor reaches 8.5, and then fails outright, with no code path or opt-out available in the affected file itself other than removing the mismarked `#[\Attribute]` or restructuring the class-like it decorates. `#[\DelayedTargetValidation]`, new in the same 8.5 release, is the one escape hatch - annotating the offending declaration with it restores the previous lazy-at-`newInstance()`-time behavior deliberately - but it is itself only usable on a PHP 8.5+ floor (there is no polyfill or conditional form of a language attribute), and choosing it is choosing to keep shipping a class that still cannot actually be instantiated as the attribute it claims to be; it postpones the failure, it does not fix it. This tool cannot observe `#[\DelayedTargetValidation]` directly or confirm the compile-time error's exact wording on PHP 8.5, since the local host is PHP 8.4.19; what is established directly is the complete pre-8.5 state this change alters - silent compilation, present-but-broken reflection data, and a `newInstance()` failure identical to a bare `new`.

Here `introduced_in` is set to 8.5 because that is the minor this compile-time enforcement actually starts in - the field exists so this behavior_change rule can be range-gated on the feature axis, and it is not a claim that PHP 8.5 introduced attributes, `ReflectionAttribute::newInstance()`, or the four class-like declaration kinds themselves, all of which predate 8.5.
notes: Runtime matrix executed on PHP 8.4.19 (2026-09-06) with `set_error_handler()` installed (no `[errno=...]` line was ever printed, confirming zero diagnostics for any of the four declarations or their decorated target classes): #[\Attribute] abstract class AbstractAttr {} plus #[AbstractAttr] class TargetForAbstract {} compiles cleanly; (new ReflectionClass(TargetForAbstract::class))->getAttributes() count = 1; ->newInstance() throws Error "Cannot instantiate abstract class AbstractAttr". The identical pattern for #[\Attribute] enum EnumAttr { case A; } => getAttributes() count = 1, newInstance() throws Error "Cannot instantiate enum EnumAttr". For #[\Attribute] interface InterfaceAttr {} => getAttributes() count = 1, newInstance() throws Error "Cannot instantiate interface InterfaceAttr". For #[\Attribute] trait TraitAttr {} => getAttributes() count = 1, newInstance() throws Error "Cannot instantiate trait TraitAttr".

Contrast, verified directly: a bare `new AbstractAttr()`, `new EnumAttr()` (via eval, since a direct `new` on an enum is a parse error, not a runtime Error), `new InterfaceAttr()`, and `new TraitAttr()`, tried outside of any attribute/Reflection machinery, throw the byte-for-byte identical Error messages as the corresponding newInstance() calls above - confirming newInstance() reaches the ordinary instantiation failure rather than raising any attribute-specific diagnostic of its own.

No automatic replacement is offered because the four target kinds require four different, context-dependent decisions rather than one mechanical rewrite: converting an abstract class to a concrete one, an interface or trait to a class, or an enum to a class are all breaking changes to how that class-like is consumed elsewhere in the codebase (implements/use/case-matching), not safe substitutions a rule can apply blindly; the alternative fix - removing the `#[\Attribute]` marking entirely - is only correct if the class was never meant to be instantiated as an attribute in the first place, which likewise cannot be inferred mechanically from the declaration alone.

PHPCompatibility 10.0.0-alpha2 was run directly (2026-09-06) via `<analyzer>/vendor/bin/phpcs --standard=PHPCompatibility --runtime-set testVersion 8.2-8.5 --report=json --parallel=1 --extensions=php --severity=1 --no-cache -q <probe-dir>` against a file declaring all four `#[\Attribute]`-on-{abstract class, enum, interface, trait} combinations and a class decorated with all four, and produced zero findings ({"errors": 0, "warnings": 0}); verification.phpcompatibility is therefore intentionally empty rather than guessed. This is the structural blindness described in the round's shared contract: PHPCompatibility's sniffs check version-availability facts about functions, constants, and syntax, not a new compile-time validation rule applied to an existing, already-available syntax combination, so a clean phpcs run gives no signal about any of the above.

Evidence: UPGRADING-8.5.0, "1. Backward Incompatible Changes" -> Core: "Applying #[\Attribute] to an abstract class, enum, interface, or trait triggers an error during compilation. Previously, the attribute could be added, but when ReflectionAttribute::newInstance() was called an error would be thrown. The error can be delayed from compilation to runtime using the new #[\DelayedTargetValidation] attribute."
